docs.title: Introduction to Algorithms
docs.text:
Welcome! This site provides clean, exam-ready notes for undergraduate students on:

  • What is an algorithm?
  • Properties of an algorithm
  • Performance analysis
  • Time complexity
  • Space complexity
  • Amortized analysis

docs.title: How to Use These Notes
docs.text:
• Read the Introduction first.
  • Then go to Performance Analysis to understand complexity.
  • Finally, practice from the Examples section.

docs.title: Learning Outcomes
docs.text:
After completing these notes, you should be able to:

  1. Define an algorithm and distinguish it from a program
  2. List and explain algorithm properties
  3. Analyze time and space complexity using Big-O
  4. Explain amortized analysis using dynamic array operations

Quick Revision

If you have an exam tomorrow, read: 1. Performance → Overview 2. Performance → Time Complexity 3. Performance → Space Complexity 4. Performance → Amortized Analysis Then solve: Examples → Complexity Examples

docs.title: Algorithm Examples
docs.text: This section gives example problems with clear algorithms and code.

docs.title: Example 1: Find Maximum in an Array
Algorithm (Pseudo-code)
docs.text:
FindMax(A):
  max ← A[0]
  for each element x in A:
    if x > max:
      max ← x
  return max

docs.title: Python Code
docs.text:
def find_max(arr):
    max_val = arr[0]
    for x in arr:
        if x > max_val:
            max_val = x
    return max_val

docs.title: Algorithm Idea
docs.text: A number n is prime if it has no divisors in 2..⌊√n⌋.

docs.title: Python Code
docs.text:
def is_prime(n):
    if n <= 1:
        return False
    i = 2
    while i * i <= n:
        if n % i == 0:
            return False
        i += 1
    return True

docs.title: Example 3: Greatest Common Divisor (Euclid)
docs.text:
\[ \gcd(a,b) = \gcd(b, a \bmod b) \] 
def gcd(a, b):
    while b != 0:
        a, b = b, a % b
    return a

docs.title: Example 4: Binary Search (Sorted Array)
docs.text:
def binary_search(arr, key):
    lo, hi = 0, len(arr) - 1
    while lo <= hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if arr[mid] == key:
            return mid
        if arr[mid] < key:
            lo = mid + 1
        else:
            hi = mid - 1
    return -1

docs.title: Complexity Analysis Examples
docs.text: Practice analyzing time and space complexity with these comprehensive examples.

docs.title: Example 1: Simple Operations
docs.text:
def example1(n):
    x = 5           # O(1)
    y = x + 10      # O(1)
    return y        # O(1)

Analysis: - 3 constant-time operations - Time: O(1) - Space: O(1)

docs.title: Example 2: Single Loop
docs.text:
def example2(n):
    total = 0               # O(1)
    for i in range(n):      # O(n)
        total += i          # O(1) × n times
    return total            # O(1)

Analysis: - Loop runs n times - Each iteration: O(1) - Time: O(n) - Space: O(1)

docs.title: Example 3: Nested Loops
docs.text:
def example3(n):
    count = 0                   # O(1)
    for i in range(n):          # O(n)
        for j in range(n):      # O(n) for each i
            count += 1          # O(1)
    return count                # O(1)

Analysis: - Outer loop: n iterations - Inner loop: n iterations per outer - Total: n × n = n² - Time: O(n²) - Space: O(1)

docs.title: Example 4: Two Sequential Loops
docs.text:
def example4(n):
    # First loop
    for i in range(n):      # O(n)
        print(i)

    # Second loop
    for j in range(n):      # O(n)
        print(j)

Analysis: - First loop: O(n) - Second loop: O(n) - Total: O(n) + O(n) = O(2n) = O(n) - Time: O(n) - Space: O(1)

Rule

Sequential operations add: O(a) + O(b) = O(a + b)

docs.title: Example 5: Different Loop Sizes
docs.text:
def example5(n, m):
    for i in range(n):      # O(n)
        print(i)

    for j in range(m):      # O(m)
        print(j)

Analysis: - Can't assume n = m - Time: O(n + m) - Space: O(1)

docs.title: Example 6: Binary Search Pattern
docs.text:
def example6(n):
    i = 1
    while i < n:
        print(i)
        i *= 2      # Double each time

Analysis: 

Iteration 1: i = 1
Iteration 2: i = 2
Iteration 3: i = 4
Iteration 4: i = 8
...
Iteration k: i = 2^k

When does it stop? When 2^k >= n
Therefore: k = log₂(n)
- Time: O(log n) - Space: O(1)

docs.title: Example 7: Halving Pattern
docs.text:
def example7(n):
    while n > 1:
        print(n)
        n //= 2     # Halve each time

Analysis: 

n → n/2 → n/4 → n/8 → ... → 1
Number of divisions until reaching 1 = log₂(n)
- Time: O(log n) - Space: O(1)

docs.title: Example 8: Nested Loop with Dependency
docs.text:
def example8(n):
    for i in range(n):          # Outer: n times
        for j in range(i):      # Inner: i times
            print(i, j)

Analysis: 

When i = 0: inner runs 0 times
When i = 1: inner runs 1 time
When i = 2: inner runs 2 times
...
When i = n-1: inner runs n-1 times

Total = 0 + 1 + 2 + ... + (n-1)
     = n(n-1)/2
     = (n² - n)/2
     = O(n²)
- Time: O(n²) - Space: O(1)

docs.title: Example 9: Loop with Multiplication
docs.text:
def example9(n):
    for i in range(n):              # O(n)
        for j in range(n * n):      # O(n²) for each i
            print(i, j)

Analysis: - Outer: n iterations - Inner: n² iterations per outer - Total: n × n² = n³ - Time: O(n³) - Space: O(1)

docs.title: Example 10: Multiple Nested Loops
docs.text:
def example10(n):
    for i in range(n):      # O(n)
        for j in range(n):  # O(n)
            for k in range(n):  # O(n)
                print(i, j, k)

Analysis: - Three nested loops, each O(n) - Total: n × n × n = n³ - Time: O(n³) - Space: O(1)

docs.title: Example 11: Array Creation
docs.text:
def example11(n):
    arr = [0] * n       # Create array of size n
    return arr

Analysis: - Array with n elements - Time: O(n) - to initialize - Space: O(n) - array storage

docs.title: Example 12: 2D Array
docs.text:
def example12(n):
    matrix = [[0] * n for _ in range(n)]
    return matrix

Analysis: - Matrix: n × n elements - Time: O(n²) - to create - Space: O(n²) - matrix storage

docs.title: Example 13: Recursion Stack
docs.text:
def example13(n):
    if n <= 0:
        return
    print(n)
    example13(n - 1)    # Recursive call

Analysis: - Recursion depth: n - Each call uses stack space - Time: O(n) - Space: O(n) - call stack

docs.title: Example 14: Recursive with Multiple Calls
docs.text:
def fibonacci(n):
    if n <= 1:
        return n
    return fibonacci(n-1) + fibonacci(n-2)

Analysis: 

fibonacci(5)
├── fibonacci(4)
│   ├── fibonacci(3)
│   │   ├── fibonacci(2)
│   │   │   ├── fibonacci(1) → 1
│   │   │   └── fibonacci(0) → 0
│   │   └── fibonacci(1) → 1
│   └── fibonacci(2)
│       ├── fibonacci(1) → 1
│       └── fibonacci(0) → 0
└── fibonacci(3)
    ├── fibonacci(2)
    │   ├── fibonacci(1) → 1
    │   └── fibonacci(0) → 0
    └── fibonacci(1) → 1

Height of tree: n

Number of nodes: ~2^n
- Time: O(2ⁿ) - exponential! - Space: O(n) - max recursion depth

docs.title: Example 15: Loop with Inner Binary Search
docs.text:
def example15(arr, targets):
    """
    arr: sorted array of n elements
    targets: array of m elements
    """
    results = []
    for target in targets:              # O(m)
        result = binary_search(arr, target)  # O(log n)
        results.append(result)
    return results

Analysis: - Outer loop: m times - Binary search: O(log n) each time - Time: O(m log n) - Space: O(m) - results array

docs.title: Example 16: Sorting in a Loop
docs.text:
def example16(arrays):
    """
    arrays: list of k arrays, each of size n
    """
    for arr in arrays:      # O(k)
        arr.sort()          # O(n log n)

Analysis: - k arrays to sort - Each sort: O(n log n) - Time: O(k × n log n) - Space: Depends on sorting algorithm

docs.title: Example 17: Decreasing Loop
docs.text:
def example17(n):
    i = n
    while i > 0:
        print(i)
        i //= 2

Analysis: - Starts at n, halves each time - Same as Example 7 - Time: O(log n) - Space: O(1)

docs.title: Example 18: Multiple Variables
docs.text:
def example18(n):
    i = 1
    j = n
    while i < j:
        print(i, j)
        i *= 2      # i doubles
        j //= 2     # j halves

Analysis: - i: 1, 2, 4, 8, ... - j: n, n/2, n/4, n/8, ... - They meet around √n - Time: O(log n) - Space: O(1)

docs.title: Example 19: Sqrt Loop
docs.text:
def example19(n):
    i = 2
    while i * i <= n:
        print(i)
        i += 1

Analysis: - Loop runs while i² ≤ n - Equivalently: while i ≤ √n - Time: O(√n) - Space: O(1)

docs.title: Example 20: Harmonic Series
docs.text:
def example20(n):
    count = 0
    i = 1
    while i <= n:
        j = i
        while j <= n:
            count += 1
            j += i      # Increment by i
        i += 1

Analysis: 

When i = 1: inner runs n times
When i = 2: inner runs n/2 times
When i = 3: inner runs n/3 times
...

Total = n(1 + 1/2 + 1/3 + ... + 1/n)
     = n × H(n)  where H(n) is harmonic series
     = n × O(log n)
- Time: O(n log n) - Space: O(1)

docs.title: Problem 1
docs.text:
def mystery1(n):
    for i in range(n):
        for j in range(i, n):
            print(i, j)
Answer

Time: O(n²)

Explanation: 

When i = 0: inner runs n times
When i = 1: inner runs n-1 times
When i = 2: inner runs n-2 times
...
Total = n + (n-1) + (n-2) + ... + 1
     = n(n+1)/2
     = O(n²)

docs.title: Problem 2
docs.text:
def mystery2(n):
    i = n
    while i >= 1:
        print(i)
        i //= 2
Answer

Time: O(log n)

Explanation: Halves each iteration, classic logarithmic pattern.

docs.title: Problem 3
docs.text:
def mystery3(n):
    for i in range(n):
        j = 1
        while j < n:
            print(i, j)
            j *= 2
Answer

Time: O(n log n)

Explanation: - Outer loop: n times - Inner loop: log n times - Total: n × log n

docs.title: Problem 4
docs.text:
def mystery4(arr):
    n = len(arr)
    temp = [0] * n
    for i in range(n):
        temp[i] = arr[i] * 2
    return temp
Answer

Time: O(n) Space: O(n)

Explanation: - Loop: n iterations - Temp array: n elements

docs.title: Problem 5
docs.text:
def mystery5(n):
    if n <= 1:
        return 1
    return mystery5(n-1) + mystery5(n-1)
Answer

Time: O(2ⁿ) Space: O(n)

Explanation: - Two recursive calls per invocation - Forms binary tree with height n - Number of nodes: 2ⁿ - 1

docs.title: Summary Cheat Sheet
docs.text: Pattern Example Complexity Single loop for i in range(n) O(n) Nested loops for i... for j... O(n²) Halving while i > 0: i //= 2 O(log n) Doubling while i < n: i *= 2 O(log n) Sqrt pattern while i*i < n O(√n) Binary recursion f(n-1) + f(n-1) O(2ⁿ) Linear recursion f(n-1) O(n) Divide & conquer Merge sort O(n log n)

docs.title: Tips for Analysis
docs.text:
Quick Rules

  1. Sequential blocks → Add complexities
  2. Nested blocks → Multiply complexities
  3. Log appears when: halving, doubling, divide-and-conquer
  4. Count loop iterations carefully
  5. Ignore constants in Big-O
  6. Keep dominant term only
  7. Different inputs = different variables

Want more practice? Check out:

  • LeetCode
  • HackerRank

Keep practicing! Complexity analysis becomes intuitive with experience.

docs.title: Complexity Examples
docs.text: This section helps you quickly compute time/space complexity.

docs.title: Example 1: Single Loop
docs.text:
s = 0
for i in range(n):
    s += i
  • Loop runs n times
  • Time: \(O(n)\)
  • Space: \(O(1)\)

docs.title: Example 2: Nested Loops (n × n)
docs.text:
count = 0
for i in range(n):
    for j in range(n):
        count += 1
  • Time: \(O(n^2)\)
  • Space: \(O(1)\)

docs.title: Example 3: Triangle Loop (1 + 2 + ... + n)
docs.text:
count = 0
for i in range(n):
    for j in range(i):
        count += 1

Total iterations: $$ \sum_{i=1}^{n} i = \frac{n(n+1)}{2} \Rightarrow O(n^2) $$

docs.title: Example 4: Logarithmic Loop
docs.text:
steps = 0
k = n
while k > 1:
    k //= 2
    steps += 1
  • Each step halves k
  • Time: \(O(log n)\)

docs.title: Example 5: n log n Pattern
docs.text:
for i in range(n):
    k = n
    while k > 1:
        k //= 2
  • Outer loop: n
  • Inner loop: log n
  • Total: \(O(n log n)\)

docs.title: Example 6: Space Complexity with Extra Array
docs.text:
b = [0] * n
  • Extra array of size n
  • Space: \(O(n)\)

docs.title: Quick Practice (Answers Included)
docs.text:
1) for i in range(n): for j in range(n*n): ... Time: \(O(n^3)\)

2) Recursion depth n Space: \(O(n)\)

3) Merge sort auxiliary array Space: \(O(n)\)

docs.title: Properties of an Algorithm
docs.text: A valid algorithm should satisfy these standard properties.

docs.title: 1) Input
docs.text:
An algorithm can take zero or more inputs.

Example

Sorting: input is an array of numbers Searching: input is array + key

docs.title: 2) Output
docs.text:
An algorithm must produce at least one output.

Example

Searching: output can be index of key or “not found”

docs.title: 3) Definiteness (Unambiguity)
docs.text:
Every step must be clearly defined and unambiguous.

❌ “Process the array” ✅ “Sort the array in ascending order using merge sort”

docs.title: 4) Finiteness (Termination)
docs.text:
The algorithm must finish after a finite number of steps.

Warning

An infinite loop is not an algorithm.

docs.title: 5) Effectiveness (Feasibility)
docs.text:
Each step must be simple enough to be executed using basic operations in a realistic amount of time.

Example

“Add two numbers” is effective “Try all possibilities forever” is not effective

docs.text: Property Meaning Input Accepts data Output Produces result Definiteness Clear steps Finiteness Terminates Effectiveness Steps are practical

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
An algorithm is a finite sequence of well-defined, unambiguous steps that takes some input and produces the required output to solve a problem.

Formally, an algorithm is a mapping:

\[ \text{Input} \rightarrow \text{Steps} \rightarrow \text{Output} \]

docs.title: Algorithm vs Program
docs.text:
Algorithm Program Idea / logic / method Implementation of the logic Language-independent Written in a specific language Focus: correctness + efficiency Focus: correctness + compilation + execution

Example

Algorithm: Steps to find maximum in an array Program: Python/C/Java code that executes those steps

docs.title: Real-Life Example: Making Tea
docs.text:
Problem: Prepare tea.

Algorithm: 1. Take a pan 2. Add water 3. Boil water 4. Add tea leaves 5. Add sugar and milk 6. Boil for 2–3 minutes 7. Strain and serve

✅ Clear steps ✅ Ends in finite time ✅ Produces output (tea)

docs.title: Find Maximum
docs.text:
Input: Array A of size n

Output: Maximum value in A

```text Algorithm FindMax(A[0..n-1]): max ← A[0] for i ← 1 to n-1: if A[i] > max: max ← A[i] return max

docs.title: What is Amortized Analysis?
docs.text:
Amortized analysis gives the average cost per operation over a sequence of operations, even if some operations are expensive.

Unlike average-case analysis, amortized analysis does not assume input probabilities. It guarantees performance over worst-case sequences.

docs.title: Why Needed?
docs.text:
Some data structures have operations that are:

  • Usually cheap
  • Occasionally expensive

Amortized analysis spreads the expensive cost over many cheap operations.

docs.title: Classic Example: Dynamic Array Append
docs.text: A dynamic array (like Python list / Java ArrayList) grows when full.

docs.title: Cost Model
docs.text:
• Normal append: O(1)
  • When full: resize and copy n elements → O(n)

So occasionally, append is expensive.

docs.title: Key Result
docs.text: Over n appends, the amortized cost per append is O(1).

docs.title: Intuition with Doubling
docs.text:
Suppose capacity doubles: - 1 → 2 → 4 → 8 → 16 → ...

Total elements copied during resizing is roughly:

\[ 1 + 2 + 4 + \dots + \frac{n}{2} < n \]

So total copy cost over n appends is O(n).

Total work: [ O(n) \text{ (normal appends)} + O(n) \text{ (copies)} = O(n) ]

Amortized per append: [ \frac{O(n)}{n} = O(1) ]

docs.title: Real-World Meaning
docs.text:
Even though a few operations are slow, the data structure is efficient overall.

Tip

This is why Python lists and Java ArrayLists are fast in practice.

docs.title: Performance Analysis: Overview
docs.text:
Many algorithms solve the same problem, but with different efficiency.

We measure algorithm performance using:

  • Time Complexity: growth of running time with input size n
  • Space Complexity: growth of memory usage with input size n

docs.title: Example: Searching
docs.text:
• Linear search: checks each element → may take n comparisons
  • Binary search: halves the search space → takes about log₂(n) comparisons (but needs sorted input)

docs.title: Best, Worst, and Average Case
docs.text:
Let T(n) be time taken for input size n.

  • Best-case: minimum time for any input of size n
  • Worst-case: maximum time for any input of size n
  • Average-case: expected time over all inputs (needs probability assumptions)

Note

In most system/software engineering, worst-case is important for guarantees.

docs.title: Asymptotic Thinking (Growth Matters)
docs.text:
We ignore machine-specific details and focus on growth trends:

  • constants are ignored (e.g., 3n and n are both linear)
  • lower-order terms are ignored (e.g., n² + n behaves like n²)

docs.title: Big-O in One Line
docs.text:
Big-O provides an upper bound:

\[ T(n) \in O(f(n)) \]

Meaning: for large n, time grows no faster than f(n) up to a constant factor.

docs.title: Common Growth Rates
docs.text: \[ O(1) < O(\log n) < O(n) < O(n\log n) < O(n^2) < O(2^n) \]

docs.title: What You Should Be Able to Do
docs.text:
1. Count loops and nested loops
  2. Recognize log behavior in divide-by-2 patterns
  3. Decide whether extra arrays/structures increase space complexity

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Space complexity is the amount of memory required by an algorithm as a function of input size n.

It includes: - Input space (space for inputs) - Auxiliary space (extra space used during execution)

Usually, we focus on auxiliary space.

docs.title: O(1) Space Example
docs.text:
def sum_two(a, b):
    return a + b

Memory usage is constant (few variables), so:

\[ S(n) = O(1) \]

docs.title: O(n) Space Example (Copy Array)
docs.text:
def copy_array(arr):
    new_arr = []
    for x in arr:
        new_arr.append(x)
    return new_arr

Extra array grows with n, so:

\[ S(n) = O(n) \]

docs.title: Recursion Space (Call Stack)
docs.text: Recursion uses stack memory for function calls.

docs.title: Example: Factorial
docs.text:
def fact(n):
    if n == 0:
        return 1
    return n * fact(n-1)

Maximum depth = n

\[ S(n) = O(n) \]

docs.title: Space-Time Trade-off
docs.text:
Sometimes we use more memory to reduce time.

Trade-off Idea

  • Using a hash table for searching uses extra memory
  • But search becomes near O(1) average time

docs.title: Quick Practice
docs.text:
1. Iterative factorial: space?
  2. Recursive factorial: space?
  3. Merge sort: space?

✅ Answers (conceptually): - iterative: O(1) - recursive: O(n) - merge sort: O(n) auxiliary array

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Time complexity measures how running time grows with input size n.

We write:

\[ T(n) = O(f(n)) \]

Where f(n) describes the growth.

docs.title: Common Time Complexities
docs.text: Complexity Name Typical Example O(1) Constant array index access O(log n) Logarithmic binary search O(n) Linear linear search O(n log n) Linearithmic merge sort O(n^2) Quadratic bubble sort O(2^n) Exponential subset generation O(n!) Factorial brute-force TSP

docs.title: Rule 1: Single Loop → O(n)
docs.text:
for i in range(n):
    print(i)
\[ T(n) = O(n) \]

docs.title: Rule 2: Nested Loops → Multiply
docs.text:
for i in range(n):
    for j in range(n):
        print(i, j)
\[ T(n) = O(n^2) \]

docs.title: Rule 3: Halving / Doubling → O(log n)
docs.text:
while n > 1:
    n = n // 2
\[ T(n) = O(\log n) \]

docs.title: Worked Example: Linear Search
docs.text:
def linear_search(arr, key):
    for x in arr:
        if x == key:
            return True
    return False

Worst case: key not found → checks all n items:

\[ T(n) = O(n) \]

docs.title: Worked Example: Binary Search (Sorted Array)
docs.text:
Binary search halves the search space each step:

\[ T(n) = O(\log n) \]

docs.title: Constant Factors and Lower-Order Terms
docs.text:
\[ 3n^2 + 10n + 5 \in O(n^2) \]

Because for large n, n² dominates.

docs.title: Mini Practice
docs.text:
Find time complexity:

  1. for i in range(n): for j in range(i): ...
  2. for i in range(n): while k > 1: k = k//2

Expected: 1. O(n^2) 2. O(n log n)
